title: Banks would release reserves for a higher repo rate, but their responses differ sharply
bank: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
summary: A five-basis-point premium on secured overnight lending would be enough for 44 of 91 surveyed institutions to expect to reduce their reserve balances. Nearly as many, 45, would leave them unchanged. The difference is important for interpreting money-market pressure. Cash might become available from some institutions well before others would consider moving it out of their Federal Reserve account. A spread alone gives little indication of how many dollars could move, how quickly, or whether the banks holding those dollars have the approvals to lend them. These are financial officers’ conditional responses collected on 18–28 September and released on 20 November. They describe neither realised transactions nor the Board’s preferred path for system reserves.

The 56 domestic and 35 foreign banking organisations that replied held around three-quarters of system reserve balances collectively. The tables generally give each responding institution one observation and exclude non-applicable responses. The coverage of reserve dollars is substantial, but a percentage of banks is a different quantity from a percentage of reserves. Seventeen respondents put their lowest comfortable balance below $1 billion and another 17 put it at $20 billion or more. That threshold is where a bank says it would act to replenish reserves, potentially by borrowing, running down other liquid assets or bidding more for deposits. Its preferred balance includes any additional cushion it wants to hold before reaching that point (questions 1–3, pp. 5–6).

Sixty-seven institutions wanted an additional cushion. Of these, 16 wanted extra reserves equal to more than three-quarters of their minimum, including six that wanted more than the minimum itself. Over half the respondents appearing in both the March and September surveys reported an unchanged minimum, with increases and decreases equally common among those that changed it. Stability of the target can itself require active management. Fifty-two institutions reported taking action to maintain their reserve balance in recent months, compared with 18 reporting little or no intervention.

What binds depends on the institution. Internal stress outflows ranked first at 41 banks and intraday settlement needs at 36. Domestic respondents more often put payments first, while foreign respondents more often chose internal stress metrics. Even if the first-ranked constraint disappeared, 35 of the 91 expected to hold just as much in preferred reserves. Another nine expected a reduction exceeding 30%. Treating a single relaxation of a liquidity constraint as releasing a fixed fraction of reserves across banks would miss both ends of the distribution. For the selected 43 banks whose minimum relative to assets had risen substantially from February 2020 to March 2026, internal stress metrics scored 4.0 out of five as an explanation. Comments included more conservative practices following the 2023 funding stress. The smaller group whose ratio fell gave no similarly dominant explanation (questions 4–5, pp. 7–9).

The clearest split is by bank type. At a hypothetical average SOFR five basis points above interest on reserve balances, 27 of 35 foreign organisations expected a reduction, against 17 of 56 domestic institutions. At spreads of ten, fifteen and twenty basis points, the number expecting a reduction across the full sample rose to 51, 62 and 63 respectively. The similar counts at fifteen and twenty conceal changes in intensity. Fourteen respondents expected to cut their own balances by more than half at twenty basis points, versus eleven at fifteen and five at five. In the opposite scenario, SOFR five basis points below reserve remuneration, 57 expected no change. An individual bank can lend cash or change its own funding mix. These responses cannot be summed to predict a change in the supply of reserves created by the central bank (question 6, pp. 10–11).

The twelve-month outlook uses a different statistic. Respondents assigned probabilities to scenarios for their own balance sheets. On average they put a 70% probability on preferred reserves staying within 5% of their current level. Flat to modest growth received the greatest average probability for assets and deposits. This is compatible with sensitivity to repo pricing in the hypothetical scenarios. The survey did not ask respondents to price the likelihood of those spreads or report a forecast of the policy rate (question 7, p. 12).

Market access determines how far price incentives travel. The survey defines an active participant as one transacting for a purpose other than testing at least monthly. Forty-one institutions borrowed federal funds actively, but only five lent them. Forty-six borrowed cash in repo and 36 lent it. Among those 36 active repo lenders, 27 put price first among constraints. By contrast, internal risk limits and approval processes were the most frequently cited first constraint among inactive federal funds lenders. Some inactive repo lenders preferred interest-bearing reserves without the credit exposure or cited the burden of building lending operations. Several borrowers preferred secured funding or Federal Home Loan Bank advances. An attractive secured spread might move money already connected to that market faster than it draws in a new participant (questions 8–12, pp. 13–21).

Weekend settlement exposes a second obstacle. The planned expansion of Fedwire Funds and National Settlement Service to Sundays and weekday holidays was scheduled for no earlier than 2028. In September, 62 banks reported increased management discussion but only three reported more liquidity-operations staff already working weekends and holidays. Thirty offered or planned additional payment or liquidity options for clients. Thirty-five of 56 domestic respondents thought at least some discount-window access on the new operating days important, against six of 35 foreign respondents. Intraday credit was already available under existing terms. The question concerned the ability to request and receive a discount-window loan, which is a separate operational capability (footnote 5 and questions 13–15).

For a portfolio exposed to short-dated funding, valuing a backstop and relying on it for end-of-day cash are different decisions. Twenty-two respondents anticipated temporarily raising reserves before weekends and holidays, 31 did not, and 38 were unsure. Only ten said their answer would change if discount-window loans were available. Just eight expected to be operationally ready to trade federal funds on the additional days. Some comments supported matching service hours, while others mentioned borrowing stigma. The survey establishes a reason for precautionary balances to persist even with longer central-bank hours. It does not specify a future weekend spread, participation rate or aggregate liquidity shortfall (questions 16–17, pp. 23–24).

questions.question: How many dollars, at which institutions, would actually reach repo at a five-basis-point premium?
questions.detail: The survey shows a large difference in willingness by bank type but reports counts and balance buckets. Compare confidential matched reserve balances and repo lending volumes, where available, with transaction-level rates on days when SOFR remains above IORB. Separate a transfer of balances between banks from a change in system reserves. The distinction determines the cash available to absorb a financing shock.

questions.question: Would a wider spread induce new lenders or chiefly larger trades by incumbent desks?
questions.detail: Very few banks lend federal funds regularly. Among active repo lenders price dominates, while inactive institutions also mention internal limits and operating costs. Participant-level volumes, approved counterparty limits and settlement cut-offs would help distinguish a reversible price response from a structural constraint. The distinction matters for positions financed late in the day when the average traded rate can hide poor execution.

questions.question: How much weekend prefunding could a usable discount window displace?
questions.detail: The domestic response suggests considerable value in the option to borrow, yet most banks could not say their reserve decision would change or said it would stay the same. Compare actual weekend outflows, pre-positioned collateral, staffed dealing hours and test-loan settlement times. The Reserve Banks’ implementation notices and subsequent survey rounds would help distinguish access on paper from cash available before a payment deadline.

questions.question: Are stress assumptions or customer payments changing banks’ minimum reserve needs?
questions.detail: Respondents can face overlapping constraints and the March-to-September comparison supplies no dollar-weighted aggregate. Match later survey responses to bank-level changes in deposit concentration, intraday payment peaks and stress-test outflow assumptions. A rise concentrated among a few large settlement banks could affect overnight rate volatility even if the median respondent leaves its target untouched.
